# Residual Reinforcement Learning

**A deterministic controller does the driving; the learned policy only outputs a bounded correction
on top of it.** The agent never has to rediscover behaviour that classical control already gets
right — it spends its whole sample budget on the part the controller gets wrong.

The trade is explicit. You give up the possibility of the policy discovering a strategy the baseline
forecloses, and you inherit every bias in the baseline. What you buy is that a random policy at
initialisation still drives roughly correctly, so early episodes produce useful data instead of
immediate termination.

## As implemented

In the `a.bhuiyan` tree of [[it-applications-in-business-and-commerce]]:

- `_baseline_action` is a full hand-written driver — heading and cross-track error terms, a curvature
  feed-forward, a per-distance braking envelope derived from the
  [[minimum-curvature-racing-line]] speed profile, grade-aware hill logic, and an rpm gearbox with
  hysteresis and a hold timer (see [[data-driven-gearing-over-hand-tuned-rpm-bands]]).
- The [[proximal-policy-optimisation]] policy's output is blended in at **±0.5** — a hard cap on how
  far the agent can deviate, exposed as `--residual-scale`.
- `_launch_warmup` brings the car to roughly 90 km/h under baseline control **before** the agent gets
  the wheel, so no episode is spent learning to start.
- `_apply_steer_constraints` adds a speed-scaled clip and a rate limit on top, so even a saturated
  residual cannot produce a physically absurd steering command.
- The observation is a **33-dimensional tracking-error state** built by
  `flatten_racingline_observation` — deviations from the precomputed line, not raw sensors. The
  policy sees "how wrong is the baseline right now", which is the only thing it can act on.

`--no-assist` disables the whole arrangement, which is how the ablation is expressed.

## The self-learning corner memory

A second, non-gradient learning loop sits beside the policy. When the car goes off track, the
environment records the arc-length coordinate, slows that corner's target speed, and **propagates the
same reduction to curvature look-alikes elsewhere on the track**. The result persists to a `.npy`
that the environment auto-loads, and `analyze_telemetry.py` can rebuild it offline from logged laps.

- **TODO:** no convergence criterion or stopping rule for the corner memory is stated anywhere in the
  repo, and nothing documents what prevents oscillation between over- and under-slowing a corner.
  `confidence: low` on its stability. Do not assert it converges.

## Outcome, stated honestly by the source

This branch's own README records that it **did not fully solve the S-curve** and that the car did not
finish a clean full lap in the earlier runs. The top-level `project/README.md` softens the same
result to "reduced but didn't eliminate S-curve errors" — one of the drift instances catalogued on
[[documentation-drift]]. The branch that shipped as the headline result is the *other* one; see
[[ship-two-branches-not-all-eight]].
